_doc: The colony: who lives at your base, what they do all day, what they eat and what they pay you. Design references (comments only, never in game text): Colony Survival for the go-to-work loop, Necesse for workers who maintain what you laid out rather than inventing it. The numbers here are the whole balance of js/colony.js — no rule lives in code that could live in this file. Hours are in-game hours; a day is 24 of them.
_scheduleDoc: A rudimentary day, deliberately. Wake, walk to the job, work it, walk home, eat, sleep. Boundaries are hours of the day; js/colony.js steps a citizen through them and nothing else decides where they are. A citizen with no job still wakes and still eats — an idle mouth is meant to be visible.
_jobsDoc: A job says which work orders a citizen will pick up (`tags`), how fast they turn hours into work units, and whether the job is allowed to CREATE anything. `mayBreakGround` is false on every job in this file and that is the Necesse rule made literal: a farmer harvests and replants the plots the player laid out, and can never lay a new one. Nothing in js/farm.js will let a citizen past that flag.

jobs.name: Labourer
jobs.blurb: Turns their hand to whatever order is nearest.

jobs.name: Farmer
jobs.blurb: Brings in what is ripe and puts the next seed in the same hole. Will not break new ground.

jobs.name: Miner
jobs.blurb: Works a face or a drill; carries ore to the nearest store.

jobs.name: Smelter
jobs.blurb: Feeds the furnaces and pulls the ingots.

jobs.name: Carpenter
jobs.blurb: Raises what you have outlined and keeps it standing.

jobs.name: Hauler
jobs.blurb: Walks the pool boundary all day so nothing sits in the wrong crate.

jobs.name: Cook
jobs.blurb: Turns raw crop into meals, which go further than raw crop.

jobs.name: Guard
jobs.blurb: Stands a post. Counts toward the base's defence, not its output.

_foodDoc: Citizens eat, and an unfed colony has to degrade in a way the player NOTICES without being a disaster they cannot come back from. Four rungs: hungry (slower), grumbling (stops paying tax), downs tools (does no work at all), leaves (walks out). Nobody ever starves to death — a dead citizen is a save-scum, a departed one is a lesson. Hunger runs 0..1 and one full day with nothing to eat is `hungerPerDay`.
_housingDoc: A bed is the whole housing model. Housed citizens sleep, recover mood and pay tax; an unhoused one sleeps rough, loses mood and pays nothing. Spare beds are also the single biggest pull on migration, which is what makes building a house BEFORE you have anybody a sensible thing to do.
_taxDoc: Gold out of people rather than out of loot. Only a citizen who is both FED and HOUSED pays — that is the whole lever, and it means the answer to 'how do I make money' is always 'look after more people'. Mood scales it, prosperity (your refined output, your waypoint, your walls) scales it again, and the cap stops a hundred peasants from replacing the game.
_migrationDoc: New people arrive because the place is worth coming to — spare beds, food in the store, walls up, and folk already there who are not miserable. Appeal runs 0..1 and is rolled against once per in-game day. A migrant is an OFFER, never an automatic arrival: they turn up at the edge of the claim and the player says yes or no, because a citizen you did not choose is a mouth you did not budget for.
_recruitDoc: The other way to get people: walk into a town and pay somebody to come back with you. A town has a small pool that refills slowly, the price climbs with the size of your colony (you are asking them to leave a working town for a hole in the ground), and good standing with whoever holds the zone knocks it down. Refusing is free.
_comfortDoc: THE CIVILIZATION EXPANSION, §2. A house is a structure with a `home` block in data/structures.json; a utility is a structure with a `utility` block. Comfort is the house's own number plus one point for each DISTINCT utility KIND whose radius reaches it — four privies is one privy — clamped to 0..1. Comfort does exactly two things and no more: it scales the mood a housed citizen recovers overnight, and it decides whether a vendor will live here. It deliberately does NOT scale work output, because a second hidden multiplier would make 'why is my furnace slow' unanswerable.

utilityKinds.warmth: a fire that is always lit

_labourDoc: §3. One work unit buys thirty seconds of a tended machine's running time. `bankSeconds` caps how far ahead a machine can be charged, so a furnace cannot be wound up for a week and left. `orderUnits` is the grain the board posts in — four units is two minutes of furnace, which is a stream of small completions rather than one enormous order.
_vendorDoc: §5. A vendor is a person who decides to live at your place because of something you did. Three gates and all three are required: the condition, a FREE BED whose comfort clears `wants`, and no offer already pending. The panel always says which of the three is short. A vendor is never a job in `jobs` above — they must never be rolled as a migrant off the road, and `jobs` is what rollMigration picks from. They occupy a bed, they eat, they pay rent instead of tax, and they put exactly zero units on the work board.

vendorJob.name: Trader
vendorJob.blurb: Keeps a stall. Pays you rent, works for nobody.

vendors.name: Quartermaster
vendors.sells: Rations, rope, torches, bedrolls and seed
vendors.buys: Anything, at four-tenths of what it is worth
vendors.blurb: The first trader who will look twice at a place like this.

vendors.name: Forge-Warden
vendors.blurb: Follows the smoke. Will not set up where nothing is hot.

vendors.name: Stonewright
vendors.sells: Cut stone, brick, concrete and the groundwork pieces, cheap
vendors.blurb: Sells the dull half of every building for less than anyone else.

vendors.name: Apothecary
vendors.blurb: Wants a quiet plot well away from the hammering.

vendors.name: Victualler
vendors.sells: Grain, cooked rations, seed and salt
vendors.blurb: Turns up the week the second field goes in.

vendors.name: Carter
vendors.sells: Hand carts, pack mules, wagons and route upkeep
vendors.blurb: Stands at the Trade Post door and tells you what a cart really costs.

vendors.name: Chandler
vendors.sells: Lamps, lanterns, lamp oil, candles and the street lights
vendors.blurb: Will only live on a street that is lit after dark.

vendors.name: Armiger
vendors.sells: Guard contracts, turret parts and ammunition
vendors.blurb: Runs the muster, and will sell you somebody to walk beside a cart.

vendors.name: Wright
vendors.sells: Machine parts, wire, control boards and the Tender Arm
vendors.blurb: The last one to move in, and the one who makes the rest unnecessary.

vendors.name: Factor
vendors.sells: Trade goods, at this place's price
vendors.blurb: Keeps the price board. Everything they touch costs a twentieth more than it should.

vendors.name: Drover
vendors.blurb: Camps outside the ring, because the animals will not settle inside it.

vendors.name: Gambler
vendors.blurb: Arrives once there is enough money here to be worth losing.

_guardDoc: §8. A post is a structure with a `post` block; a guard is a citizen standing in one. A posted guard counts as a point of defence exactly the way a turret does, which is what makes 'spend gold on people' a real alternative to 'spend materials on walls'. One stat block, read by your guards AND by a town's, so the two are never quietly different. Nobody dies: a guard who falls in a raid is knocked down and is back at their post the next morning at half mood.
_awayDoc: §4. Production does not stop when you leave. js/logistics.js's away clock already runs the machines and the carts forward; this block is the half it does not cover — the people, the fields and the trade runs — plus the caps. `rate.closed` is under 1 so that closing the game is not straightforwardly better than playing it; it is a fudge and the away card says so. The REAL cap is the crate: catch-up runs the actual machines against the actual pool, so a furnace with forty ore in reach makes twenty ingots and then says it is waiting for ore. Nothing anywhere invents an input. `mercyDays` holds hunger at the grumbling rung after three game days, because losing your village for taking a flight is a punishment for playing.
_musterDoc: §9. A drill is an ordinary raid with a flag on it, run through js/raid.js so every rule the raid already keeps — nothing spawns before the bell, night is harder and pays more, the rare crate is a floor — keeps itself for free. Cooldown is per RANK and per PLACE, so clearing rank 4 does not lock out rank 1. Losing costs nothing at all beyond whatever dying already costs you: no broken structures, no materials taken, no citizen leaves, no standing lost. The user's words: 'No need to penalize for a minigame.'
_tradeDoc: §7. What a thing is worth somewhere is its base price moved by whether that place NEEDS the tag and whether it MAKES it, plus a slow wobble on a six-day step. Clamped hard, so the whole spread a player can ever see on one good is about three and a half times — enough to be worth a cart, never enough to be a slot machine. A place never both needs and makes the same tag; `makes` wins.
_carrierDoc: §7.5. A carrier is a row in a table — how much it holds, how fast it goes, what a trip costs in upkeep and how many guards may walk with it. Three of the five are already in data/power.json's hauler table with these exact capacities and speeds and are repeated here ONLY with the trade fields; the haulage numbers themselves still belong to that file.

carriers.name: Porter
carriers.blurb: One person and a pack. Slow, cheap, and always available.

carriers.name: Hand Cart
carriers.blurb: The first real load. Four times a porter for twice the money.

carriers.name: Pack Mule
carriers.blurb: Faster than the cart and it eats.

carriers.name: Covered Wagon
carriers.blurb: Slow, enormous, and worth robbing. Take the four guards.

carriers.name: Hauler Drone
carriers.blurb: Faster than anything that wants to rob it, and it dies with the grid.

_holdDoc: §6.5. The hold is the ONE capped container in the game, and the weight limit is the entire reason trade is interesting. There is no encumbrance: going over the limit is impossible rather than slow, and the panel says 'the cart is full, three of seven went in'. `onBack` is the same forty kilograms data/resources.json's haul block already uses.
_namesDoc: Plain invented names, built from syllables so the colony never repeats itself and nothing here belongs to anybody else. A game that already has Name Forge can pass its own `makeName` into createColony and this table is ignored.
_r18Dead: R18 — a number stated in two files is a number that will be tuned in the wrong one, which this round has now fixed four times (structures/power prices, the generator kW, the logistics pole's radius, and these). `food.cookedMealMultiplier` removed: the live one is data/crops.json's `cook.multiplier`, read by js/farm.js. Same value, 1.6, in two files — and only one of them was ever read. the `muster` block removed: js/muster.js reads `D.muster || civics?.muster` where `D` is data/raids.json, so raids.json's block always won and this one never applied.
